image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Two-line chart with shaded area between the lines** (a band/range-style line chart).

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single panel** chart.
- Uses **two overlaid lines**.
- Uses **shaded fill between lines** to emphasize the gap/advantage.
- Includes **direct annotations/labels** on lines and regions.
- No faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Parents’ income rank | Ordinal | Position on x-axis |
| Estimated admissions advantage / likelihood of admission relative to average | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Legacy status / scenario (legacy applicants vs. without legacy status) | Categorical/nominal | Separate line color (dark vs. light gray), line identity, shaded gap between lines |
| Average admissions rate | Quantitative (reference value) | Horizontal baseline/reference line with label |
| Selected percentile labels (10th, 30th, 50th, 70th, 90th, 99.9; “Top 0.1%”) | Ordinal | Axis tick labels and annotation text |

comments.raw_comment: From the graph, I noticed that legacy applicants have a significantly higher admissions rate across the board (over twice the average rate). However, those wither higher parental income had a proportionally larger benefit: up to 7 times the average for the top 0.1%, compared to less than triple (already high) for non-legacy. This leaves several burning questions: among them, why are admissions so heavily skewed in favor of high-income, legacy applicants, and what steps can colleges take to reduce this (likely-systematic) bias?

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that students with a higher income and legacy parents were more likely to be admitted. This could be for a variety of factors such as the fact that hire income families don't require scholarships and have access to more tutoring and educational resources, therefore getting better grades and more likely to give the school mor money. These reasons should not cause an equally hard working student with less resources, less connections, and less money, but of the same intelligence to not be admitted. Unfortunately this is not the case. It is also important to note that statistics can be very easily skewed and data is hard to collect 100% accurately so we still do not know the exact statistics and factors that go into these decisions.

comments.raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I can see that, for legacy applicants, applications of those with a family income rank of more than the 50th percentile essentially stays at a rate of 2.5 times as likely or more to be accepted. However, I'm noticing that non-legacies with an income rank of about 85% are under 1 times as likely to be accepted into an elite college. 

After analyzing the graph, I wonder how these admissions numbers will be impacted over the next several years. After the Supreme Court case in June that eliminated affirmative action in terms of college admissions on the grounds of things like race, I'm curious to see how this will extend to legacy statuses. Legacies aren't necessarily considered to be disadvantaged, but non-legacies may be, so it'll be interesting to see if legacy admissions rise or drop. 

This graph doesn't necessarily affect my immediate community very much, as I don't know anyone who was aiming to be accepted into a highly selective college. However, I do live in the general proximity of Rice University, which is a very selective college that likely exhibits admissions bias based on whether someone is a legacy and the income bracket that they are in. 

A headline that captures the graph's main idea might be "Application Distortion: Legacies vs. Everyone Else."

comments.raw_comment: It was interesting to see how much a student's legacy can effect their acceptance rate, especially for students of parent's with higher incomes. For students of parents who have a mid to high income, legacy has a significant boost on their acceptance rates. I wonder why legacy is so important to these colleges. Parents and their children can differ significantly in character traits and personalities, which makes the idea of legacy a questionable way to admit students. If these colleges' goal is to attract and accept the most intelligent, talented, and skilled students, why is such an emphasis placed on legacy? It seems irresponsible of these colleges to accept based on legacy and unfair to the multitude of highly talented students who are rejected because they lack legacy.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that for legacy applicants, they are 7x as likely to be admitted as opposed to applicants without legacy status, meaning that if an applicant had relatives with a history of attending a certain elite university such as Ivy Leagues, then they had a much higher chance of being accepted compared to an applicant who did not have any prior legacy status in their family. Also, the richer an applicant's parents' income rank was and the more upper class they were, the higher the chance they were to be admitted into an elite college, even under the scenario of students with the same test scores. 

I wonder why it's harder for applicants without legacy status to be admitted into the same university with the same scores as others who have family or are a apart of generations in their family that have a history of attending the elite college that they are currently applying too. While I do understand why generations of a family might wish to all attend the same prestigious school, I don't think it's fair to other applicants who work just as hard but are simply the first of their family to apply and wish to be admitted. However, I think that this current statistic very likely has to do with elite colleges wishing to keep their students "elite", and the fact that most legacy status applicants most likely come from wealthy families that are able to use connections and legacy history to their advantage.

comments.raw_comment:
Apart from the stand-out jump in the admission rate for legacy applicants of the 99.9% income percentile, I found it interesting that the admissions rate was higher for non-legacy applicants of the <50% income percentile than it were for the 50-95% higher income percentile of those applying. Interestingly enough, the admissions rate for the same income brackets of legacy applicants do not follow this trend but rather continually get higher until reaching the extremes.
I wonder of what the admissions graph would look like if instead of using the income percentiles, the graph used fixed yearly salaries. According to what I saw in the bottom of the page, the 99 or 99.9 percentiles represented those with an income of 620k+, I would be interested to see how admissions rates change in the millions or tens/hundreds of millions range. I believe that this graph relates to Texas in the way that many students in this state, regardless of socioeconomic status, do not even apply to out-of-state colleges in the first place. Many students are happy to stick with applying with their regional legacy schools. As being from an immigrant family in Australia with no prior experiences of the American College system, I find it interesting regarding the state boundaries that many confine themselves to as the equivalent state/province boundaries in Australia are nowhere near as considered. For a title: "Elite Admissions Opportunities Impacted by Socio-Economic Status."

It's a similar fallacy for all highly selective schools - if a school only allows in the best students (for whatever meaning of best you like), the school and it's teachers don't have to be any good, because the best students will excel regardless.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that whether a person is a legacy or not makes a huge difference for upper middle class people. It is the hardest for this group to get in without legacy. The acceptance chance for the super wealthy is much higher regardless of legacy or not, though significantly higher with legacy.

I wonder why politicians are so concerned with the “unfair advantage“ that affirmative action gave when legacy acceptances are conveniently overlooked. “Shouldn’t we reward people based on their hard work and not luck of the draw?” A familiar argument used this past summer when affirmative action was overturned. But is being a person of color “luck of the draw”? Or is being a legacy, the majority of which are white, wealthy individuals not upholding systemic inequality?

I know a lot of legacy students and a lot of students who have been admitted into top 20s/Ivies on merit. Most of the legacy students I know are white, privileged, and relatively less accomplished than those who aren’t. In no way am I saying that legacy students are not as smart or as talented, but there is a clear favor towards these students.

“Lucky in Legacy: An Ivy’s four leaf clover”

Money makes the world go around, and colleges are businesses, so income is their main focus. The more wealthy can provide this, especially when their multigenerational legacies and alumni of these institutions. I would title this graph: "College Admissions: Money Talks."

comments.raw_comment:
This graph compares students with the same test scores and how their chances of being admitted to elite colleges can fluctuate based on their legacy status and their parent's income rank. It is clear from this graph that in every income rank, legacy status helps boost admission. I find it insane that very wealthy people with legacy status are 7x more likely to get into a school than a poorer person without status who worked just as hard to get the same scores. I wonder why there is such a bias in college admissions. One reason for this bias is that wealthy families may donate a lot of money to the school which could put applicants at an advantage. However, one would assume that by having all this wealth, one already has an advantage in life. Therefore, giving a wealthy and a poor person who both have legacy status and have the same scores unequal opportunities is solidifying those societal norms. Also the poor students not getting into these elite colleges because they are put at an inherent disadvantage when applying, it is further hindering their opportunities in life. I wonder if giving out financial aid is one of the reasons that poorer students who have the same credentials as wealthy students have a less likely chance of getting into a school. I know that financial aid is limited. This affects me because I will be applying to colleges soon. Some schools are doing away with legacy status, so I am not sure how much this graph will affect me. 
"Legacy Boost= Bias"

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it is measuring the relation between parents’ income, legacy status, and admissions status at the collegiate level. I noticed that, generally, richer applicants had a greater estimated legacy boost than those who were poorer. For example, as the parents’ income rank became closer and closer to 100th, the estimated legacy boost became closer and closer to 7x. Whereas, on the other hand, poorer applicants closer to an income rank of 10th seemed to only have an estimated legacy boost of 2x. I wonder if the legacy boost is greater for applicants whose parents have a higher income rank because having a richer background increases the chances of multiple generations of family members being able to afford attending that college. Additionally, I noticed that the estimated advantage in admissions for those without legacy status on the richer end of the spectrum was lower than for those who were poorer and wonder why this is the case. I also wonder what criteria and processes a school uses to determine their legacy boost discrepancies and if this varies from college to college. This applies to my community because I recently went through the college process and the concept of legacy advantage has been a concern for many. It can be unfair as applicants can have very similar profiles to legacy applicants yet those with legacy are favored over them. My headline for this graph would be: “Is Bias Overcoming the College Admissions Process?”.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that legacy applicants have a significant advantage in the college admissions process over people applying without a legacy status to elite colleges. However, I also noticed that it is 7 times more likely that a legacy applicant to an elite college would be admitted if their parents’ income is higher than the 90th percentile. Additionally, I find it interesting that there is a dip in the graph for applicants without a legacy status in which the parents are around the 70th percentile in income. This is intriguing because parents with a relatively low income (in the “poorer” income rank) were two times as likely to be admitted. With this, I noticed and wondered why the “poorer” and “richer” extreme income rank almost reached the same likelihood of admittance for non-legacy applicants. Furthermore, I wonder how the graph would appear individually for each of the elite colleges (which elite college favors more legacies overall?). The graph relates to my community because as a senior, I along with many of my classmates are going through the college admissions process. This makes me wonder how money and legacies will affect my classmates’ admissions to certain colleges.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that students with legacy status and whose parents’ income rank is in the top .1% are 7 times as likely to be admitted to a given school compared to a non-legacy student who is not incredibly wealthy. I also notice that people without legacy status who are incredibly wealthy have a much greater advantage than non-legacy students who have lower incomes. I wonder why these elite colleges place so much emphasis on financial status. If these families are already wealthy why should they be given even more advantages in life than they already have? Why do these schools not attempt to give opportunities to people who may not have a lot of money but have the potential to be incredibly successful if they are given the opportunity to study at a prestigious university? It is very likely that these legacy families donate large sums of money to the universities and continue to do so as their children and their grandchildren get accepted. These donations provide the university with significant benefits and could be a very likely reason why they choose to admit legacy students who are very likely to attend and who have parents who will provide continuous donations to the university during and after their time there. If they choose not to accept a legacy student they may lose some of their best donors, and prestigious universities make incredible amounts of money from their donations and would not want to lose these funds. -unifished see other post

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that legacy students of all income rankings tend to see significantly higher admission rates than non legacy students. To a certain extent, income also seems to be a determining factor in admission rates. Students with family incomes ranking in the top 10% are much more likely to be admitted than those in the bottom 10%. 

The fact that students are more likely to be admitted when their family income is higher is interesting. Many colleges claim to be need-blind when looking at college applications, so the data has to be due to other factors possibly influenced by higher income. Students with more resources have easier access to information, tutors, or other outside assistance. These resources are likely to positively impact their academic performance and college applications. However, students with less resources end up disadvantaged in comparison to these students.

This graph sheds light on how a student’s family background — something they have no control over — can impact their lives. A student whose family has a higher income and more access to resources will typically end up more successful than one with a lower income. As a community, students with less access to resources needed for academic excellence need to be addressed. If we can address this issue, we can reduce the disparity between legacy and non-legacy, or high-income and low-income.

This graph depicts the likelihood of admissions advantages at some colleges compared to those with the same test scores and a legacy advantage. I also noticed that regardless of income, legacy applicants were admitted significantly higher than those without legacy status. I noticed that students who have a legacy advantage are more wealthy compared to those without a legacy advantage. I wonder how this could be and why there is a lesser legacy for students with low income. Maybe it could be because the wealthier applicants can afford high tuition costs and donate money to the elite college whereas the low-income ones would struggle and would request financial aid.  I wonder how income and legacy advantages affect a student getting into an elite college in the admission process. Like if you request financial aid are you more likely to be deferred or rejected? This affects me and my community because I am a sophomore who is starting to research college so next year I will be applying and looking at schools. Also, I have 2 older sisters who have applied to colleges without a legacy advantage and got in. But my family friend with a legacy advantage for Villanova as her uncle went there, got differed.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph shows the relationship between elite colleges and their tendency to choose applicants based on economic status and family legacy. The black line (legacy applicants) is significantly higher than the gray line (non-legacy applicants), indicating that elite schools favor legacy. Legacy applicants appear to automatically have double the chance of acceptance. It also is apparent that both types of applicants have a spiked chance of getting into an elite college when their parent’s income surpasses the 90th percentile. One thing that stood out to me was that applicants without legacy status who fall into the middle-class range have less of a chance of getting into an elite college versus an applicant with poorer or richer incomes. Do colleges discriminate against middle-class applicants because they are not rich enough to generate a lot of money but not poor enough to even out their statistics in appearing to be a school that caters to all financial statuses? This relates to me because as a current senior applying to college, I have had to witness students get into colleges just because of their legacy status and or because their parents have a higher income. Even though we may have the same statistics, colleges will always choose the legacy/richer applicant. This has hurt all students, not just me, and our disadvantage when it comes to being a middle class without legacy status when applying to elite colleges. 

“College: The Legacy of a Rich Man’s World!”

-The applicants with parents on the wealthier end of the spectrum who are not legacies are less likely to get accepted then poorer non-legacy applicants.

comments.raw_comment:
1)
I notice that there's about a 2x boost for legacies of any kind, and that it stays constantly above the non-legacy line. I also notice that the extremely wealthy legacies, ie; the 0.1 percentile are nearly 7x more likely to be accepted. Considering that elite colleges have an acceptance rate of about 3.3% to 7.3%, the acceptance rate for rich legacies is about 23.1% to 51.1%. This is important because traditionally, people who go to elite colleges are more likely to be rich in the future. The boost given to wealthy people and to legacies is meant to keep the class divide obvious and the school selective. 
 
2)
I wonder if this legacy boost exists in every single college. What would happen if each college had an individual graph plotting the difference between legacy and non-legacy? Does this bias go on to affect other things at the college, like grades, clubs, etc? Why is there a dip in the graph at around 50th and below the 90th?  What is it about these top 0.1 percentile legacies that makes colleges so incredibly drawn to them?

3)
This relates to my and my community because I am planning to go to college one day, and being a middle class non-legacy, it feels discouraging to apply to Ivy League and other elite schools. And even if I were to get accepted into these schools, many of the people I would be attending with would also be extremely wealthy, leading to a difference in experience and in values. 

4)
"Are You Rich? Are You a Legacy? Welcome to Harvard!"

It is very discouraging to realize that even though my peers and I are very educated and intelligent our application to elite colleges are looked differently than of an application that comes from wealth.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
The very first thing I noticed while looking at the graph is how much more likely legacy students are to be admitted into college. There is a significant trend indicating how legacy students are far more likely to be admitted into ivy league colleges. The second thing I noticed is how rich-non legacy kids are less likely to be admitted compared to poor-non legacy students. The third thing I notice is how the percentage of rich-legacy students have the biggest advantage in getting into the Ivy League.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the admission officials care so much about legacy. Does it increase profit? I also wonder why more wealthy kids who have no legacy have less of a chance of being admitted into college. 

How does this affect me and my community?
My classmates and I are going to be starting the college process very shortly and knowing the chances with legacy and whatnot can be a huge factor. It makes many students ask the question- “do I have less of a chance of getting into a college because I have no legacy and no wealth”? It seems to create an unfair advantage to me and my community which is very concerning to some.

Headline
Wealth and legacy- is this mainly what admissions care about?

1) I notice that legacy students have a greater chance overall of being admitted into elite schools than students without the status. After the 50th percentile, while the chances to get admitted for legacy students went up, it had gone down for students without the status. Students without the status chances of being admitted had decreased the richer their families were, even going below average until after the 90th percentile of parents' income rank as their chances rose again. 

2) Why is the legacy status valued more? Why did the chance of being admitted decrease so much for normal students between the 70th and after the 90th percentile of parents' income? How many students hold the legacy status in these schools?

3) As many people are applying to college, it seems rather unfair that they'll have fewer chances of being admitted if they don't have the legacy status. As applying to elite schools is already very competitive, it is a great disadvantage as normal students also do the hard work getting the same grades, yet have less chances of getting in. When in all ways, students with legacy status always have the benefit of the doubt if they'll get in or not.

4) The College Admission Game: Perks of Being Legacy Status

I noticed that there is a significant gap between the legacy boost and the estimated advantage without the legacy boost. Even without the legacy boost the graph shows that when you are in the 99.9 percentile of your parents' income rank, you are still around 3x more likely to be accepted into an IV school. 

I wonder if students ever have an issue with this and sometimes feel that they just got into these schools because of their parents. I feel like I would feel that I didn't deserve to be there and I would want to get into the school on my own. I also wonder if the parents will notice this and begin to do something about it or if they just do not care enough. 

This relates to me because I will be soon applying to colleges and it is interesting to learn more about statistics. It is interesting to learn that my community is middle-upper class and that diminishes our chances of getting into an IV league school. It is kind of frustrating to learn that income is a part of being accepted into college, while it should be about your education levels and many other things not including your parents' income.

comments.raw_comment:
Notice:
Admission spikes for the top 0.1% regardless of a student's legacy status. 
For poorer students, the admission gap between legacy and non-legacy applicants is fairly stable. For applicants above the fiftieth percentile, legacy students have a much higher advantage. 
Admittance of non-legacy students dips after the 70th percentile and spikes again around 99.
Non-legacy students have the best admittance if either above the 90th percentile or below the 50th: upper/middle-class students don't have great chances unless legacy. probably because neither in need of financial aid nor willing/able to fund programs. 
Wonder: 
Other than test scores, legacy status, and parental income, what factors are considered? How would extracurriculars, GPA, and other factors change this? - many schools no longer consider test scores (especially elite colleges). 
Relate: 
As a high school student, I am fairly anxious about college admissions. I've seen a lot of people with really impressive applications who weren't accepted into the schools they wanted. I know someone personally who graduated high school in 2022 with good grades, great test scores, and a year in an exchange program and still got in almost nowhere she applied. 
Headline: 
No Legacy, No Money, No Luck: Bias in College Admissions

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that when applying for colleges, out of everyone with the exact same test score, legacy students are over twice as likely to be admitted. Furthermore, out of those legacy students, the children whose family has a higher income and makes more money are chosen above the others. A legacy student with a family income in the 99th percentile is 7x more likely to be admitted than the average student with the same test scores. 
I wonder why the colleges are prioritizing financial status when students apply for college. Why has our country’s education system turned away from helping educate students and form capable adults? Why is making more money a bigger priority than equality? I wonder how and if we can fix this inequality. Our country is based off of the idea of equal opportunity, and yet this is anything but equal. 
This affects me as an upcoming senior looking into colleges. It is discouraging knowing that no matter how much I study, other students will still have an unfair advantage. This affects my research in which colleges I might apply to. Knowing I might have a better chance as a legacy student is unfair, but an advantage that some might not help but to exploit. Knowing this data is frustrating, yet it is an advantage to be well informed going into college searches. 
“College Acceptance : the turn from equality and opportunity to moneymaking and legacy”

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that students with parents who have a higher income are more likely to be accepted. While the bottom 50% are about 3x as likely to be accepted, while it climbs quite tremendously in the top 50%. It escalates to the summit where the top 0.1% are 7x more likely to be admitted. I also noticed that without a legacy boost, the top 0.1% has about the same chance to get in as the bottom 10% with a legacy boost. I wonder if this happens because kids with wealthier parents have more money for better education. I also wonder if it has to do with dropping out because of mental illness which can be more common in poorer accommodations. This relates to me and my community because while I go to a school that offers scholarships and is welcoming no matter how wealthy the family is, I know many people don't live like that. Many students get bullied for how much or little money they have. This graph shows the bias in our community toward the wealthy, often because they are able to afford a better education. While people may think that that's fair, it's not really because the parents of these children likely work just as long if not longer than the top 0.1%. The difference is that the top 0.1% was able to make a money harvesting company that the lower class people may not have been able to do because of the bias in society. To sum up, we have a bias in our community because of poverty status
Headline: College Admission: How do they show the bias in our community?

comments.raw_comment:
Noticed: The chart is carefully crafted to support a kneejerk reaction that rich legacy applicants are getting admitted at the expense of poor applicants. Looking closer, I notice non-legacy applicants below the 40th income percentile have about 1.75 x the average non-legacy admissions rate. These applicants will likely need a lot of financial aid, due to the bloated cost of college. So the colleges accept a larger proportion of legacy applicants, particularly at the higher income levels. The colleges know that statistically, these applicants’ families will donate large amounts, that can be redistributed down to the 40th percentile and below. Legacy admission advantage and lower-income admissions advantage are the yin and yang of college admissions. At first glance, colleges appear to be acting as Robin Hoods, taking from the rich and giving to the poor. But looking deeper, they are really acting as Grifters – Bloating up their staff and salaries, then stealing from the rich to give to the poor, then demanding the poor turn the money over to – the colleges’ bloated staff and salaries!
It's disappointing but not surprising that The NY Times, which sees victimhood everywhere, cannot bring itself to delve deeper into this to provide a comprehensive, fair analysis.
